actors.plain: Actors give a map's objects a class and identity. Components give each object individual jobs, with rules that prevent invalid combinations.
actors.analogy: A door is the Actor; its placement and creaking sound are separate components. One prop, several responsibilities.
flow: Choose a placeable class
Edit compatible components and properties
Cook bounded native instances
details: 3D, 2D and UI have distinct root contracts.
C++, Blueprint and Lua classes share reflected identity and type checks.
Component creation is filtered by owner-domain and compatibility rules before it modifies an Actor.
actors.tip: Start with one simple Actor. Composition is a tool for clarity, not a contest to attach the most components.

migration-actors.plain: Projects from the Entity and Behaviour era require deliberate recreation in the Actor model. Projects already created with v0.1.1 Actors remain compatible with v0.2.0.
migration-actors.analogy: This is rebuilding a set on a stronger stage, not pressing a button that silently rewrites the old scenery.
flow: Preserve the old project
Create a current Actor-based project
Copy source assets and rebuild maps and scripts deliberately
details: Legacy documents are rejected with an explanation and are not rewritten in place.
Logical ownership and spatial attachment remain distinct.
Map 6, Blueprint 5 and reflection schema 9 remain current in v0.2.0.
migration-actors.tip: Keep the original project and a version-control checkpoint until the recreated game has built and run successfully.

worlds-2d.plain: 3D, 2D and UI are three editing spaces in one map. The 2D world is made of Actor2D nodes measured in pixels with Y pointing down, and it runs natively on the console between the 3D world and the HUD.
worlds-2d.analogy: A side-scroller's character lives in the world; the health bar lives on the screen. They should not share an accidental coordinate system.
flow: Pick the space the object belongs to
Place it in the matching Scene mode
Play it on the console
details: 2D positions, collider sizes, velocities and camera limits are all pixels; rotations are degrees.
2D nodes carry sprites, tile maps, bodies, cameras, paths, particles, skeletons, navigation and joints.
A project without 2D nodes compiles none of the 2D runtime.
worlds-2d.tip: Switching view modes does not convert an Actor or delete objects hidden by the domain filter.

scene-blueprints.plain: A Scene Blueprint coordinates the objects and events of one map. It runs as a single map-owned SceneScriptActor rather than a manually placed object.
scene-blueprints.analogy: Actors are the cast. The map script cues this particular scene's performance.
flow: Open Map Settings
Edit the map's graph and local references
Compile and test that scene bank
details: Only SceneScriptActor subclasses qualify as map scripts.
Local references use stable identity and type checks.
Reusable object logic belongs in Actor/Component classes; map-specific coordination belongs here.
scene-blueprints.tip: Keep reusable door logic in the door class, not copied into every level's opening sequence.

music-sequences.plain: Choose resident effects, native MIDI music with a SoundBank, or a disc stream. The guide shows how each route is imported, assigned and controlled from the editor, Blueprints, C++ and Lua.
music-sequences.analogy: MIDI is the sheet music; the SoundBank is the instrument case. The SPU stage has only 24 chairs, shared with sound effects.
flow: Import the score and instruments
Analyze and save a PSX recipe
Compare previews, then test the game
details: SF2/SF3 libraries keep their source snapshots; conversion selects required regions and layers.
Compact/Balanced/High presets and an opt-in optimizer help fit budgets without silently dropping instruments.
A host Target Preview does not reproduce hardware interpolation, interrupt latency or all runtime contention.
music-sequences.tip: Reserve room for menu clicks and gameplay SFX before giving the entire SPU to the orchestra.

native-hud-preview.plain: Native C++ menus can construct themselves automatically in the UI editor through a dedicated preview hook, without launching a PSX build.
native-hud-preview.analogy: See the completed menu set before the opening curtain animation starts. The actors do not need to perform the whole play for a layout check.
flow: Share UI construction code
Inspect the automatic edit preview
Interact optionally, then verify on target
details: A separate native process runs construction hooks; normal edit preview does not run gameplay lifecycle.
The desktop and console paths share Q12 HUD layout and primitive generation.
Blueprint logic, real audio/cards, scene loading and cycle-accurate performance are outside this preview.
native-hud-preview.tip: Use UI mode, not world 2D. Earlier instructions used the old two-mode label.

iteration.plain: Build manually, reuse only verified output, select a small group of scenes and inspect both static memory and runtime timing before adding more content.
iteration.analogy: The memory report is the packing list; the Debug HUD is the lap timer. A light suitcase does not guarantee a fast race.
flow: Choose scenes, target and data source
Build or reuse a matching receipt
Measure the actual target workload
details: Source observation invalidates stale output without automatically compiling a PSX game.
Debug HUD metrics describe specific intervals or memory use; they are not additive hardware utilization percentages.
Persistent serial control and dependency repair keep their ownership, acknowledgement and cancellation boundaries.
iteration.tip: Position interpolation smooths motion; it does not create more FPS.

lua-tutorial.plain: Create a real Actor class in Lua, expose properties in the Inspector, move it every tick and build the same source through any of Epok's three execution modes.
lua-tutorial.analogy: The Lua file is a typed gameplay blueprint written as text: its declared shape is inspected before any code can run.
flow: Create and declare one class
Add typed properties and lifecycle methods
Place the Actor, choose a mode and test it
details: The file name, local class name and returned class must agree.
Properties are literals or explicit Epok constructors, not arbitrary file-scope expressions.
The epok-lua v1 profile is intentionally smaller and more predictable than general Lua.
lua-tutorial.tip: Start in Native C++ mode with the small Spinner example. Switch modes only after the same class compiles and behaves correctly.

lua-scripting.plain: The Lua reference defines the exact class syntax, type system, engine builtins, diagnostics, execution modes and limits shared by every Lua project.
lua-scripting.analogy: Think of it as the language contract at the border: every value must have a size and meaning that the PlayStation runtime can honor.
flow: Declare the class shape statically
Compile one typed intermediate representation
Run native code or a bounded VM backend
details: Lua classes can inherit from reflected C++, Blueprint or Lua parents.
Generated epok.d.lua definitions keep external editor tooling aligned with the live registry.
Mode changes invalidate incompatible build artifacts and never trigger a silent fallback.
lua-scripting.tip: When a diagnostic rejects ordinary Lua, check the profile table before trying to work around it dynamically.

lua-vm-runtime.plain: The VM guide explains what each Lua mode links, how much target memory it reserves, and how host-cooked bytecode is proven compatible with the 32-bit runtime.
lua-vm-runtime.analogy: Native mode translates the recipe before shipping; bytecode ships a compact prepared recipe; source mode also brings the parser into the tiny kitchen.
flow: Select one project mode
Build the matching archive and script payload
Measure the fixed arena and target result
details: Bytecode defaults to a 96 KiB arena and source to 128 KiB.
The ABI verifier compares host and target chunk headers byte-for-byte.
Lua 5.2/psxlua MIT notices apply only when a VM archive is linked.
lua-vm-runtime.tip: Choose by measured game needs: source mode is convenient but carries the parser and the largest reserved arena.

release-v0.4.0.plain: Version 0.4.0 adds terrain you can sculpt, navigation your characters can follow, and a Native PC runtime that runs the same gameplay code on your computer before it ever reaches a console.
release-v0.4.0.analogy: It fills in three gaps at once: the ground to walk on, the way to find a path across it, and a rehearsal room so you can watch it before opening night.
flow: Review compatibility and the editor version
Try the new template browser and gameplay flavors
Sculpt terrain, bake navigation, iterate on Native PC
details: Every authoring contract from v0.3.0 is unchanged: no project recreation, scene migration or asset rewrite.
A project descriptor must declare editor_version 0.4.0; upgrade through the Hub, which backs up the descriptor first.
New projects choose a template, a gameplay flavor (C++, Blueprint or Lua) and a target platform as independent choices.
Appending a variant to a reflected enum or a member to a record no longer breaks saved Blueprint graphs.
The gameplay API reaches 485 public operations, each implemented on C++, Blueprint and all three Lua execution modes.
Terrain, navigation and the Native PC runtime have not been validated on physical PlayStation hardware.
release-v0.4.0.tip: Start with the compatibility section. The one thing you must do to an existing project is let the Hub move its editor version forward.

release-v0.3.0.plain: Version 0.3.0 made one gameplay surface behave identically in C++, Blueprints and Lua, added a timeline sequencer with a live scene preview, and replaced software music with a native driver for the PlayStation's own sound chip.
release-v0.3.0.analogy: Three authors, one script: whichever language writes the scene, the performance on the console is the same one.
flow: Review compatibility
Adopt the unified gameplay operations
Re-cook music for the native driver
details: Projects kept map format 6 and Blueprint format 5; no recreation or scene migration was required.
The Lua gameplay profile advanced from 1 to 2, adding composite values, service operations and typed foreign receivers.
Timeline assets advanced from schema 2 to 3, adding optional per-track sections with time remapping.
Epok Pulse compiles a MIDI entirely on the host into an absolute-timestamped SPU command stream; the software synthesizer stayed selectable as a reference.
Skeletal triangles gained per-corner texture coordinates and the per-model clip limit rose to 32.
release-v0.3.0.tip: If you author music, compare the Target Preview against the software reference before committing to the native driver.

release-v0.2.0.plain: Version 0.2.0 brings Lua into the same gameplay model as C++ and Blueprints, adds two skeletal target formats, and tightens several authoring workflows.
release-v0.2.0.analogy: It adds a third language to the same stage: the cast, props and runtime stay shared even though authors can write, wire or script the performance.
flow: Review compatibility
Choose the features relevant to your project
Run the required release validation before upgrading
details: v0.1.1 Actor projects did not need another document migration.
Lua Native C++ mode links no VM; the bytecode and source modes do.
Skeletal models gained a choice between direct GTE bone ranges and compressed baked vertex frames.
Physical-hardware validation of Lua and the new skeletal paths remained pending.
release-v0.2.0.tip: Read the compatibility section first, then follow the focused guides for whichever features you actually intend to use.

release-v0.1.1.plain: Version 0.1.1 unified scene authoring around typed Actors, improved Blueprint creation and compilation feedback, and switched new Third Person projects to progressive output.
release-v0.1.1.analogy: It is the release where the scene stopped being a list of entities and became a hierarchy of typed objects you can reason about.
flow: Migrate existing scenes to Actors
Re-check Blueprint compilation feedback
Confirm your project's display mode
details: Scene documents moved to the typed Actor model; the older Entity and Behaviour format was retired.
Progressive PlayStation output avoids the interlaced motion artifacts visible on physical displays.
Existing projects keep their saved resolution; the change applies to newly created Third Person projects.
release-v0.1.1.tip: This is the oldest release with notes on this site. Projects older than it need the Actor migration before a current editor will open them.

dungeon-tutorial.plain: A guided first dungeon: create the Dungeon template, play it, roll new seeds, change the route and the look, add a minimap, pick a seed that fits and let game code ask where things are.
dungeon-tutorial.analogy: You are the architect who chooses the rules; the generator is the construction crew that builds a new site every time you change your mind, and never complains.
flow: Create and play the Dungeon template
Change the recipe, the style and the seed
Add the minimap, test seeds, query from code
details: The template uses the Third Person character in a recipe dungeon with stairs, caves, a key, a locked door and a handmade room.
Every generation is one undo step, and the band shows the console budget before you build.
Keys and doors work the same in C++, Blueprint and Lua.
dungeon-tutorial.tip: Press New seed freely: Ctrl+Z brings back the dungeon you liked better.

dungeon-rooms-tutorial.plain: Build a room by hand once, save it as a Dungeon Room, and let recipes place it in every dungeon turned to fit its corridors. Then use volumes to keep the generator away from art of your own.
dungeon-rooms-tutorial.analogy: Like a prefab room in a modular building kit: you design one module carefully, and the builder fits it into any floor plan through its doors.
flow: Build the room under one actor, with Door markers
Save it and mark doors and spots on its floor plan
Add it to a Handmade rooms step and generate
details: Plain meshes, cubes and solid colliders merge into the dungeon; lights and scripted actors are copied.
Rooms turn in quarter turns, and doors nobody uses are walled by the style.
Keep out and Only here volumes work with recipes; Room here and Mirror with rooms-and-corridors layouts.
dungeon-rooms-tutorial.tip: Keep At most small: every quad of a map costs console RAM, even inside a beautiful room.

platformer-tutorial.plain: A guided first 2D game: create the Platformer 2D template, play it, paint new level from tiles and turn a picture into a crate that falls, bounces and gets pushed.
platformer-tutorial.analogy: Think of the template as a furnished flat: you can live in it as it is, repaint a wall, or move in your own furniture one piece at a time.
flow: Create and play the Platformer 2D template
Paint level with tiles and terrains
Add a rigid body and fix its warning
details: 2D units are pixels with Y pointing down, like the screen.
Tile collision comes with the tiles you paint.
Warnings in the Hierarchy and Inspector name what a node needs, often with a one-click fix.
platformer-tutorial.tip: Delete the template groups you do not need early: it frees RAM and makes the Hierarchy yours.

release-v0.7.0.plain: Version 0.7.0 adds the Dungeon Generator: seeded dungeons in 3D and 2D with designed routes, keys and locked doors, stairs, handmade rooms, gameplay queries, a minimap, a seed bench and volumes, plus a Dungeon template.
release-v0.7.0.analogy: It is a level designer that never sleeps: you write the rules once, and it builds a new, solvable dungeon for every seed you try.
flow: Review compatibility and the editor version
Create a Dungeon project or add a generator to a map
Shape it with recipes, styles, rooms and volumes
details: Every authoring contract from v0.6.0 is unchanged; maps without a generator load as before.
A project descriptor must declare editor_version 0.7.0; upgrade through the Hub, which backs up the descriptor first.
Lua == and Blueprint Equal now compare object references by identity, as C++ already did.
The sample game's static RAM goes from 976.0 KiB to 981.0 KiB.
Dungeon content has not been validated on physical PlayStation hardware.
release-v0.7.0.tip: Start with Your first dungeon: the template shows every new feature working together before you build your own.

release-v0.6.0.plain: Version 0.6.0 is about 2D games: a complete 2D world on the console, a pixel-accurate 2D editor with tile painting, and a playable Platformer 2D template, plus HUD check boxes, sliders, colour tags and string tables.
release-v0.6.0.analogy: It adds a whole second floor to the house: the 3D world stays where it was, and a 2D world now lives on top of it with its own stairs.
flow: Review compatibility and the editor version
Create a Platformer 2D project
Paint tiles and add 2D nodes
details: Authoring contracts are unchanged; Actor2D nodes, TileSets and string tables are additive.
A project descriptor must declare editor_version 0.6.0; upgrade through the Hub.
The 2D runtime is opt-in by content: a project without 2D nodes compiles none of it.
The 2D world has not been validated on physical PlayStation hardware.
release-v0.6.0.tip: Play the template before reading the reference: every node it uses is explained by its own Inspector.

release-v0.5.0.plain: Version 0.5.0 is about large worlds: geometry streamed from disc in checked pages, camera visibility tracks, prepared packet order for static scenery, textures cooked to their real size, worlds beyond ±128 units and a HUD authored in the editor.
release-v0.5.0.analogy: Like a stage crew that only builds the scenery the audience can see from each seat, and swaps it while the play goes on.
flow: Review compatibility and the editor version
Pick the optimization techniques your world needs
Measure with the memory and performance tools
details: Every technique is opt-in with a stated cost; a project that enables none builds as before.
A project descriptor must declare editor_version 0.5.0; upgrade through the Hub.
Rebuild after upgrading: texture placement and baked face formats change generated output.
release-v0.5.0.tip: Read World optimization first: it says what each technique does, when to use it and what it measured.
